Linux live analysis: architecture and acceptance contract

by Alexander Panasenko · xrefcode.com

  10. L3: bounded hardware data watchpoints (DR0–DR3) and dependent watches (--follow)
  11. L4: opt-in PID-pinned live MCP tool (xref_live)

Status: implemented across Stages L1 (PR #49), L2 (PR #53), L3 Increment 1 (PR #54), L3 Increment 2 (PR #55), and L4 for issue #46. Available starting with v0.3.0; the published v0.2.0 and earlier binaries do not contain xref live or the opt-in xref_live MCP tool.

For a recorded, step-by-step example with real commands and their output (memscan → resolve → refs/c → probe → watch → --follow after a buffer move), see the Live Analysis walkthrough, also published at xrefcode.com/live-walkthrough.

The goal is to connect a running Linux x86-64 process to XRef's static address/function evidence: find state, observe selected calls, and identify candidate instructions that modify selected memory. Each result must distinguish an observation from an inference and state its coverage and limits.

Delivery order

  1. L1: process identity, mappings, address resolution and memory search. Use safe standard-library reads, bounded output and controlled synthetic target processes. This is the first independently reviewable deliverable.
  2. L2: function hit counts, followed by caller/register evidence. Validate the Linux tracing adapter on a synthetic fixture before adding it.
  3. L3: hardware write watchpoints. Validate event/IP/value semantics and thread/resource coverage separately; preserve unknowns.
  4. L4: explicitly enabled live MCP. Add a PID-bound live context only after cancellation, process lifetime and backend cleanup have been validated.

The issue remains open while requested later stages are outstanding. Source changes use isolated worktrees, focused development tests, a completed-change final gate, independent review and explicit integration. Implementing L1 does not imply publishing a new release or tracing a production process.

Architecture and platform boundaries

  • Preserve the existing static Analysis, JSON queries and default xref_query MCP contract: one immutable selected image.
  • A separate live ProcessContext owns the selected PID, lifetime/executable identity, mapping observations and read handles. A request cannot silently redirect that context to another PID.
  • Keep unsafe_code = "forbid" in the project crate. L1 can use std::fs and Unix FileExt::read_at; later tracing uses an optional, validated Linux adapter. Avoid a mandatory new debugger or BPF compiler.
  • Initial live support is Linux x86-64 with an ELF executable. Preserve macOS host builds and report unsupported_platform for unavailable live commands. Existing static Mach-O support is a separate capability.
  • Keep modules focused and below the source-size limit. Suggested boundaries: CLI/types, proc parsing, process identity/I/O, ELF/load-map resolution, scanning, word classification and rendering.

L1: identify the process and translate addresses

Stage L1 (maps, resolve, memscan) command shapes:

Command
xref live maps --pid PID --json
xref live resolve --pid PID LIVE_VA... --json
xref -b app.elf live resolve --pid PID LIVE_VA... --json
  1. Validate the PID. Open and retain proc/executable handles, record the PID's start identity and executable identity, and hash the actual executable bytes. A numeric PID alone is insufficient because a PID can be reused.
  2. If --bin is supplied, verify it identifies the process's executable build. An identical copy can be accepted by digest; a coincidental filename cannot. Resolve the executable automatically when no binary path is supplied. Static commands retain their requirement for a selected binary.
  3. Read bounded maps/smaps metadata. Preserve paths as reported, including spaces, escape spelling and deleted-file suffixes; paths are labels rather than authority to open arbitrary files.
  4. Obtain ELF load-segment geometry and flags. Do not infer executable status from the existing Segment { va, offset, size } fields alone.
  5. Distinguish static VA, file offset and live VA explicitly. Check the relevant load segment, its file-backed extent, mapping identity and load bias. Never apply one unexplained global subtraction to every mapping.
  6. Preserve multiple valid interpretations as candidates. Bytes in an anonymous mapping or a zero-filled segment tail are not automatically file-backed code.
  7. Recheck process/executable identity at operation boundaries. Report process exit, replacement, image mismatch and mapping changes explicitly; do not quietly attribute data from a changed process to the original image.

Return raw addresses and mapping provenance when static function attribution is unavailable. An .eh_frame FDE range is not proof of a source-level function.

L1: search memory and show a compact context window

Proposed command shape:

Command
xref live memscan --pid PID U64_VALUE... --before-words 2 --after-words 6 --max-hits 32 --json

The input is a bounded sequence of little-endian u64 values. Matches start at 8-byte-aligned live addresses. Limit pattern length, requested/read bytes, result count, context words and total serialized output.

Region selection and scanning

  • Default to eligible private anonymous/heap/stack mappings and verified private data mappings of the selected executable. Skip shared/device/IO/PFN and unclassified mappings with an explicit reason. Missing flags are not proof that a special mapping is ordinary RAM.
  • Scan in bounded chunks. Keep enough overlap to match a pattern crossing a contiguous chunk boundary, without emitting duplicate hits.
  • Treat short reads, inaccessible pages, mapping changes and EOF separately. Do not bridge an unreadable gap with overlap bytes, fabricate zero-filled data, or report a complete negative result after skipping unreadable memory.
  • Use checked address/length arithmetic. Recovery from an unreadable span must advance and remain bounded; it must not retry forever at the same address.
  • Check the deadline between reads. Standard proc-memory reads can block in the kernel, so this is a cooperative elapsed-time budget, not a hard real-time timeout. Report actual elapsed time and the stop reason.
  • Memory changes while it is being read. The result is an observation during an interval, not an atomic process snapshot or a claim that a source object has been reconstructed.

Context window and pointer hints

Return a compact window of aligned words around each match, rather than an unbounded memory dump. The proposed defaults are two words before and six words after, with at most 32 hits. These are upper bounds: output/region/read limits can shorten a window or stop the result earlier, and that loss must be visible.

Each slot carries its address, exact observed word when readable, classification and evidence. Serialize 64-bit addresses/words without losing integer precision. Do not silently read across an excluded mapping or guard gap to fill a window.

Candidate classifications:

  • code_ptr: the value maps to the selected executable and a recovered static range; include live/static VA and range provenance. Otherwise retain an executable-mapping pointer without inventing a function identity.
  • Pointer to a known static pointer/relocation or read-only region: provide the relevant evidence. This alone does not prove a C++/Rust vtable or object type.
  • Static data pointer: optionally preview bounded ASCII from verified file bytes, distinguishing that preview from bytes read from live memory.
  • Heap/stack/mapped pointer candidate: report the containing mapping. Mapping membership does not establish allocation ownership or object bounds.
  • Scalar/unclassified word: retain the actual value. An unreadable or partial word has a separate status and must not become a scalar zero.

Result and failure contract

The human CLI and JSON output share the same typed live result. Keep a versioned envelope with tool/version, operation, process/image identity, observation interval, mapping identity, data/error, warnings, coverage, limits and stops. The existing static JSON/MCP schema does not silently acquire arbitrary PID access.

Examples of necessary distinctions:

  • permission_denied versus an empty match list;
  • process_exited/process_changed versus an image that has no matching code;
  • unreadable/skipped memory versus memory that was examined and did not match;
  • budget/result/output exhaustion versus a complete result for the stated scope;
  • a mapping/pointer candidate versus a recovered source type or exact past value.

The live reader does not write target memory or start/restart the target. Permissions remain governed by Linux; do not automatically elevate privileges or change host policy when an access check fails.

L1 validation and integration

Use deterministic public fixtures and a controlled synthetic Linux process. That fixture may grant the test reader access to its own memory; the product must not change another process's ptrace policy as part of attachment.

Acceptance covers:

  • maps/stat parsing, unusual path/comm spelling, malformed/overflowing metadata and absent/duplicate mapping flags;
  • identity changes, process exit and image mismatch;
  • PIE and non-PIE VA/file/live translation, segment permissions, file-backed boundaries and ambiguous or unmapped addresses;
  • known patterns, multiple hits, alignment, chunk boundaries, unreadable gaps, deduplication and compact window truncation;
  • byte/result/output/time stop reporting and permission failures;
  • existing static CLI/MCP behavior and an explicit unsupported-platform result.

Run only new/directly affected tests during implementation. Follow the repository's final formatting/lint/compile gate and reuse successful checks on unchanged code. Independent review must inspect the actual diff and evidence, not just an exit code.

L2: bounded uprobe hit counts, caller evidence and register samples

Stage L2 (probe) command shape:

Command
xref live probe --pid PID ADDR... [--backend perf|tracefs] [--count] [--callers] [--regs] [--duration-ms 1000] [--max-events 4096] [--json]
xref live probe --backend tracefs --pid PID ADDR... --fetch 'amount=+0x30(%rcx):u64' --filter 'amount > 0' --every 2 --first 64 --until-hits 128 --json
xref live probe --backend tracefs --pid PID ADDR... --duration-ms 0 --heartbeat-ms 1000 --group-by ret --mark-file /tmp/app.log --mark-regex '^TX-[0-9]+'
  • Target verification: requires a verified (dev, ino) executable match and resolved PIE slide (--force-bin mismatches cannot install verified uprobes), an executable file-backed PT_LOAD (PF_X) offset, and an iced-x86-verified instruction boundary inside a known FDE/symbol anchor.
  • Primary backend (--backend perf, default): opens per-TID dynamic uprobe PMU counters (/sys/bus/event_source/devices/uprobe/type) via perf_event_open with an mmap circular binary ring buffer (PERF_RECORD_SAMPLE, PERF_RECORD_LOST, PERF_RECORD_FORK), mm-filtered (pid_isolated_breakpoint: true) to the target process, dynamically attaching newly spawned threads and automatically releasing kernel probes when xref closes its file descriptors.
  • Explicit tracefs adapter (--backend tracefs): uses an isolated instance under instances/xref_<pid>_<nonce> (pid_isolated_breakpoint: false because inode-wide int3 traps fire across processes sharing the inode before tracefs filtering), two-pass /proc/<pid>/task seeding, event-fork + record-tgid, explicit exclusion of fork descendants (other TGIDs), O_NONBLOCK trace_pipe draining, per_cpu/cpu*/stats loss summation (overrun, commit overrun, dropped events, or unknown), FD-close-before-rmdir teardown, append-only -:group/event unregistration, and a process_group(0)-isolated parent-pipe cleanup supervisor subprocess so foreground process-group SIGINT (Ctrl-C), SIGTERM, or abort cleans up dynamic events.
  • Tracefs fetch and sampling options: repeat --fetch NAME=EXPR up to 16 times (bounded register or nested memory fetches such as amount=+0x30(%rcx):u64). --filter FIELD OP INTEGER accepts only numeric comparisons over fetched values or fields enabled by --regs; the predicate is installed in the tracefs event and checked again while reading. --every N selects every Nth matching event per probe, --first N caps recorded hits per probe, and --until-hits N stops after N accepted hits across the session. These options require the explicit --backend tracefs; fetched values print beside register samples and appear in JSON fetched_samples. Sampling counts are marked as lower bounds; stored fetch output is capped and reports truncation. When multiple addresses are probed, fetch lines include the static probe VA prefix (va 0x... fetch ts=...), while single-probe sessions preserve the compact fetch ts=... format. Fetch labels accept register names when not conflicting with --regs or fetch syntax; reserved names (reserved: ra) are rejected with clear diagnostics.
  • Unbounded probing and heartbeats: --duration-ms 0 enables unbounded mode, running until --until-hits, target process exit, or SIGINT/SIGTERM (Ctrl-C). The first signal ends the observation and still prints the report and --group-by histogram; a second signal exits immediately, and the tracefs watchdog removes the probes. Optional --heartbeat-ms N periodically prints status to stderr with total hits collected, target liveness, and elapsed time since the last hit. --json-lines (either backend, any duration) prints one JSON object per accepted hit as it happens — va, tid, fetch (tracefs), ret (static return site, when known) and mark — and ends with one {"report": ...} line carrying the full report (counts, coverage, groups). --json keeps the single aggregated report; the older --backend tracefs --duration-ms 0 --json form still streams hits.
  • Caller grouping: --group-by ret aggregates hits into a histogram keyed by caller return site ([rsp] static VA, symbolized with function names), summarizing fetched values per group.
  • Mark file tracking: --mark-file PATH --mark-regex RE tails a log or state file and stamps each probe hit with the matching line that was current at the hit (e.g. current transaction ID or span). RE supports literals, ., [...]/[^...], \d \w \s (and \D \W \S), ^, $ and the * + ? quantifiers; alternation, groups and {n} repetition are rejected with an error rather than silently matching nothing. The file is polled every loop iteration (about 5 ms) and each new line is recorded with its CLOCK_MONOTONIC observation time; a hit gets the latest line observed at or before its trace_clock=mono timestamp, so a line written after the hit is never attached to it, even when tracefs delivers the event later. A line is timestamped when xref reads it, normally within one ~5 ms poll of being written but later if the observer is delayed (scheduling, event backlog), so a line written shortly before a hit can still show up on the next hit. The last 1024 marks are kept; a hit older than that history gets no mark rather than a later one. tracefs backend only, together with --fetch, --regs or --json-lines (where the mark is printed).
  • A full probe_ready receipt is emitted once. Later thread changes are compact tid_attached/tid_observed stderr records; JSON stores them in the separate observation.thread_changes array (attached for perf, observed for tracefs).
  • Capability matrix & zero silent fallback: JSON and table outputs report a shared capabilities block (requested, available, collected, detail for hit_counts, timestamp_ns, tgid_tid, callers, registers, and pid_isolated_breakpoint), truncated_by_max_events, and raw_register_bits_do_not_prove_source_types. Neither backend ever silently falls back to the other on EACCES/EPERM.
  • Unwind & caller attribution: evaluates the effective CIE + FDE unwind row at the probe PC (CFA == RSP + 8 and RA == Offset(-8) at standard entries, or explicit RSP/RBP frame offsets), attributes callers via return_static_va - 1, and verifies the preceding CALL instruction with iced-x86, preserving raw return addresses and explicit tail-call/unwind caveats.

L3: bounded hardware data watchpoints (DR0–DR3) and dependent watches (--follow)

Stage L3 hardware watchpoint command shape:

Command
xref live watch --pid PID [ADDR...] [--follow SPEC]... [--len 1|2|4|8] [--access write|rw] [--regs] [--duration-ms 1000] [--max-events 4096] [--json]
  • Target validation (1..=4 total hardware slots): enforces the x86-64 DR0–DR3 limit (<= 4 hardware watchpoint slots per session across fixed ADDRs and --follow chains), natural alignment (runtime_va % len == 0 for len in 1 | 2 | 4 | 8), mapped region bounds, and writable permission for --access write (rw-p). Accepts either live runtime VAs (heap, stack, anonymous, or static data) or static ELF VAs mapped via PIE slide.
  • Dependent watch model (--follow ptr_slot=<ADDR>[,offset=<OFF>][,len_slot=<ADDR>,min_len=<BYTES>][,guard_slot=<ADDR>,guard_val=<U64>][,header_ptr_slot=<ADDR>,header_offset=<OFF>]):
    • Reserves 2 hardware slots for a single-hop chain (1 write watch on ptr_slot + 1 watch on the resolved leaf *ptr_slot + offset) or 3 hardware slots when header_ptr_slot is also watched (total_slots <= 4).
    • Re-evaluates the pointer chain via a bounded two-pass /proc/<pid>/mem consistency check (MAX_REBIND_SNAPSHOT_RETRIES = 3), never trusting a sample's written_value as a proven new pointer.
    • Records rebind_events across initial_bind, in_place_resize, relocated_buffer (disabling/closing old leaf DR samplers and opening new samplers at generation + 1), and disarmament (disarmed_null_or_unmapped, disarmed_bounds_violation, disarmed_guard_mismatch, disarmed_torn_read, lost_header_binding) so freed or reused heap allocations are not attributed to the disarmed watch.
    • Reports rebind_coverage_gap: true, counts_are_lower_bound: true, and root_liveness (assumed_live_without_allocator_proof or guard_verified_without_allocator_proof) with explicit caveat leaf_rebind_uses_two_pass_proc_mem_read_never_sample_store_value_and_cannot_prove_allocator_lifetime_without_guard.
  • Per-TID PERF_TYPE_BREAKPOINT + PERF_SAMPLE_REGS_INTR: opens per-thread hardware breakpoint counters (HW_BREAKPOINT_W or HW_BREAKPOINT_RW) with mmap binary ring buffers, dynamically attaches newly spawned target TIDs via PERF_RECORD_FORK and /proc/<pid>/task, and automatically releases DR0–DR3 when xref closes its file descriptors.
  • Post-execution trap_ip vs candidate_writer_static_ip: x86-64 data watchpoints trap after the store/access instruction commits (trap_ip points to the next instruction). xref caches the decoded enclosing FDE layout on first hit (WriterStaticCache), rejects function/symbol boundaries, intra-FDE direct branch/call targets (ambiguous_branch_target), and non-fall-through predecessors (Call, IndirectCall, UnconditionalBranch, IndirectBranch, Return, Exception), verifies effective-address overlap against the watched range, and reports the local linear predecessor as a candidate (candidate_linear_predecessor_store or candidate_linear_predecessor_read) with the explicit caveat candidate_linear_predecessor_store_operand_assumes_no_indirect_or_cross_fde_entry.
  • Candidate store-operand value decoding vs memory snapshots: decodes written_value as candidate_register_store (using the 16-GPR PERF_SAMPLE_REGS_INTR snapshot at trap delivery) or candidate_immediate_store for mov [mem], reg and mov [mem], imm instructions under the same explicit no-indirect-entry caveat; read-back from /proc/<pid>/mem before and after observation is reported separately as initial_snapshot / latest_snapshot with latest_proc_mem_snapshot_not_store_time_value.

L4: opt-in PID-pinned live MCP tool (xref_live)

Stage L4 opt-in MCP startup command:

Command
xref -b app.elf mcp --allow-live-pid PID
  • Strict opt-in & default isolation: without --allow-live-pid PID, xref -b app.elf mcp exposes only the read-only xref_query tool (readOnlyHint: true, destructiveHint: false, idempotentHint: true, openWorldHint: false), and any tools/call for xref_live is rejected with JSON-RPC -32602 ("unknown tool").
  • Startup identity pinning: when --allow-live-pid PID is supplied, xref validates PID != 0, opens /proc/<pid> with force_bin = false, verifies verified_build_id or verified_sha256 against --bin, and pins (pid, starttime_ticks, exe_dev_ino) in LiveMcpContext. If startup validation fails (dead PID, non-Linux host, Mach-O binary, or binary mismatch), the process exits nonzero before writing anything to stdout.
  • No PID/binary redirection & lifecycle safety: LiveQuery (maps, resolve, memscan, probe, watch) uses #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] and intentionally omits pid, bin, and force_bin. Every xref_live invocation re-verifies starttime_ticks and exe_dev_ino via open_pinned_session; if the pinned process exits or its PID is reused, xref_live fails with a structured process_exited or process_changed error (isError: true) while static xref_query calls remain available.
  • Tight MCP budgets, serialization & cooperative cancellation:
    • Caps MCP timeout_ms / duration_ms at 1..=5000 ms, max_hits at 1..=64, max_bytes at 1..=268435456 (256 MiB), max_events at 1..=4096, resolve addresses at 1..=64, probe addresses at 1..=16, and total watch hardware slots (addresses + follow) at 1..=4 (DR0–DR3).
    • Serializes xref_live execution so at most 1 live operation runs at a time (returning error.code == "busy" on concurrent xref_live requests), while sharing the server's 2-request total admission cap and 64 KiB MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES response envelope (LiveToolResponse).
    • Honors notifications/cancelled and stdio EOF across memscan, probe, and watch loops (ProbeStopReason::Interrupted), ensuring immediate perf FD closure and tracefs teardown.

Sampling profiles

On Linux x86-64, profile a verified executable and a running process with hardware performance events. The kernel and system policy must permit the requested events; unavailable events return an error rather than silently changing the event or backend.

Command
xref -b ./app live profile --pid "$PID" --duration 10s --freq 4000 \
  --callers dwarf --out capture.xprof
xref -b ./app profile report capture.xprof --by function --top 30
xref -b ./app profile report capture.xprof --by block
xref -b ./app profile report capture.xprof --by line
xref -b ./app profile annotate capture.xprof 0x1234 --json
xref -b ./app profile annotate capture.xprof 0x1234 --c
xref -b ./app profile diff before.xprof after.xprof --other ./app-new --json
xref -b ./app profile import perf.data --out imported.xprof --base 0x400000 --pid "$PID"

--callers dwarf unwinds a bounded captured user stack with CFI from the target and verified shared objects; incomplete unwinds are reported and can omit callers when a module or its CFI is unavailable. fp uses kernel call chains, lbr needs supported hardware and provides a bounded branch history, and none records leaf samples. Shared-library addresses are attributed to their module when mappings are known; a file hash is a snapshot of the backing file, not proof of unchanged in-memory code. Line reports need DWARF line information; stripped images may leave samples unresolved. Pseudo-C statement attribution is approximate and separately reports unmapped samples.

--trigger-probe 0x1234 --window 200ms uses a bounded in-memory flight recorder around a uprobe hit. Thread attachment, buffer eviction and asynchronous events can leave gaps; lost and dropped records, incomplete coverage, and the trigger status are reported. The capture thread CPU measurement excludes costs incurred by the target and interrupt contexts, so it is not a measurement of the total workload slowdown. Sample shares are not exact execution time.

Importing text from perf script, or binary perf.data directly, currently requires --pid and either a caller-supplied runtime image --base or --maps snapshot. The base or snapshot and target identity are unverified, mappings are synthetic, and timestamps or event periods may be missing. Native import preserves recorded sample periods, timestamps and loss records when present, but cannot prove the target identity or recover all mappings. For recordings with multiple event types, it imports the first and marks the report incomplete. It accepts bounded zstd-compressed perf records, including bounded AUXTRACE records in compressed streams. A supported Intel PT stream can be decoded from an AUX-only capture or alongside one ordinary sampled event. Reconstructed instruction events are reported separately from CPU samples: they do not measure elapsed time and have no reconstructed timestamps. The importer requires a matching build ID and executable mapping and currently rejects multi-thread or CPU-wide PT streams, loss, unsupported packet sequences, and ambiguous image mappings. Other AUX formats remain undecoded and mark a sample report incomplete; an unsupported AUX-only capture cannot be profiled. Runtime code modifications cannot be ruled out from perf metadata. The PT integration has been tested with synthetic trace bytes, a compiled ELF and real perf sideband, not with a hardware Intel PT capture. Mixed profiles currently support function, instruction, block, caller-path and line reports; folded output, annotations and profile diffs reject them. For this initial decoder, record a per-thread user-mode trace and restrict the PT address filter to executable code in the selected target, for example:

Command
perf record --per-thread -e intel_pt/mtc=0/u \
  --filter 'filter 0xSTART/0xSIZE@/path/to/target' -p "$PID" -- sleep 1

Replace START and SIZE with the file-relative executable range supported by the host's perf address filter. CPU-wide streams, transitions outside the verified target and unsupported packet sequences are rejected. Reaching the instruction or callchain budget retains the decoded prefix and marks it as incomplete with intel_pt_instruction_budget_exhausted. Sample-READ records with the basic grouped or single-value formats are accepted; their counter values are not included in the profile. Unsupported READ format flags are rejected. Compressed streams use a maximum 64 MiB zstd window and each compressed record may expand to at most 64 MiB. Input is limited to 16 GiB, feature metadata to 64 MiB and each perf event round to 64 MiB or 131,072 records; exceeding a limit returns an error. Native import first makes a private temporary copy of the input, so it needs temporary disk space up to the input size and may take longer on large files. Reports mark imports incomplete rather than asserting equivalence with a native capture. For a recording or snapshot made on a different system, use --target-path to identify the target's original path.

Native perf imports can infer the target slide from initial executable MMAP2 records when --base and --maps are omitted. The target path and ELF segment layout must match; if the binary was moved, a unique matching recorded build ID can identify its original path. Ambiguous slides, paths or changed mapping identities are rejected. The recorded mappings and build ID cannot prove that runtime code bytes remained unchanged. profile report --within FUNCTION_OR_VA keeps matching call chains; profile annotate --percent function --min-samples N shows function-relative shares and counts. --hz, --duration-ms and --callgraph are available on live profile; profile diff --by function --min-delta 0.5% filters small absolute changes in sample share.

For multiple post-trigger windows, use --trigger-probe VA --window-ms 500 --max-windows 20. Add --trigger-fetch 'op=+40(%sp):u64' --trigger-filter 'op == 1' to evaluate a named value captured by a tracefs uprobe at the hit. The latter requires writable tracefs and perf tracepoint access. Report a single window with profile report FILE --window 1, or their union without double counting overlaps with --merge-windows; either can be combined with --within. Trigger captures use .xprof schema 4: the schema 3 layout (window records) written by a capture with the system-wide trigger. This version reads schemas 1–4; older versions cannot read schema 3 or 4. A trigger profile with schema 3 or lower may come from per-thread triggers, so its report keeps the trigger_misses_threads_shorter_than_the_proc_poll_interval warning. Sampling is enabled only after the observer receives a matching trigger, so the beginning of a window can be missed; profiles explicitly mark this coverage limitation and report trigger losses. The trigger is a tracefs uprobe read system-wide (one perf sampler per online CPU, filtered to the target process), so it fires in every thread that executes the code, including threads created after attach and threads that exit right after the hit. CPU samplers still attach per thread once a thread is seen, so a thread that exits within that latency adds no samples to its window (trigger_window_samples_miss_threads_that_exit_before_attach). Without writable tracefs or system-wide perf access (root or CAP_PERFMON) a --trigger-probe capture fails with that reason; there is no per-thread fallback, so every saved trigger profile was taken with the system-wide trigger. Hits drained from several CPU rings are applied in timestamp order, so --max-windows keeps the earliest triggers. Existing centered single-trigger captures remain available with the original --window option.

The existing opt-in xref_live MCP tool also accepts the profile operation for the pinned process with the same 5-second duration and 4096-event caps. Its capture buffer is bounded to 16 MiB and the existing response-size cap applies.

Bounded call trace windows (live trace)

xref live trace (issue #111, discussion #110) records ordered, thread-scoped call trace windows on Linux x86-64 using the isolated tracefs uprobe backend (trace_clock=mono, set_event_pid + event-fork, record-tgid, and the out-of-process cleanup watchdog):

Command
xref live trace --pid PID \
  --start 0x1000 \
  --start-filter "op == 1" \
  --stop-return 0x1000 \
  --callees-of fn_a --depth 2 \
  --fetch-at 0x1000 "op=%di:u64" \
  --fetch-ret 0x1020 "rv=%ax:u64" \
  --max-windows 4 --max-events 1024 --duration-ms 0 \
  --json

Window lifecycle, static probe expansion and bounds

  • Start and gating (--start, --start-filter, --fetch, --fetch-at): --start VA (repeatable, static or runtime VA) opens a trace window on the thread (tid) that hits it. --start-filter PRED uses the same numeric predicate syntax as live probe --filter over --fetch / --fetch-at values attached to the start probe; non-matching start hits open no window and record nothing. When --stop (without --stop-return recursion balancing) is used on a dedicated start PC, predicates are also pushed down into the kernel events/.../filter file.
  • Closing a window (--stop-return vs --stop): Exactly one of --stop-return VA or --stop VA is required. --stop-return installs a uretprobe on the matching --start function and closes the window when its outermost activation on that thread returns (recursive re-entries increment and decrement depth inside the open window). --stop VA closes an active window on the same thread when execution reaches VA.
  • Traced callees (--callees-of FN --depth N and --functions VA,VA,...):
    • --callees-of FN --depth N (N in 1..=16, default 1) expands xref's static call graph from FN (symbol or VA) up to depth N, placing entry uprobes on static call / tail-jump instructions and post-call return-site uprobes on the verified instruction boundary immediately following each non-tail call. Tail jumps leaving a function are marked [tail] ("tail_call": true) and preserve stack depth without expecting a dedicated return-site probe.
    • --functions VA,VA,... attaches function entry uprobes (recovering and verifying the caller call site via .eh_frame / entry rsp unwind, PIE slide removed) plus best-effort uretprobe return probes. Any session using uretprobe (--stop-return or --functions) sets return_mode to uretprobe_best_effort or mixed_uretprobe_best_effort and emits the process warning uretprobe_returns_are_best_effort_under_unwind because longjmp / C++ or Rust stack unwinding can bypass return trampolines.
  • Value attachment (--fetch-at, --fetch-ret): --fetch-at VA "NAME=EXPR,..." attaches values on --start, --stop, --functions entry, or --callees-of call-site probes matching VA (either the call-site VA or callee entry VA). --fetch-ret VA "NAME=EXPR,..." attaches values on the return probe (uretprobe or post-call return site) of VA. Colliding kernel fetch names on shared PCs (such as adjacent call instructions) are automatically aliased in uprobe_events and restored in the output.
  • Ordering and bounds (--max-windows, --max-events, --duration-ms): Events are isolated per tid and ordered by trace_clock=mono nanosecond timestamps (program order within a thread across CPUs). Reaching --max-windows or --max-events, --duration-ms (0 = run until limits, target exit, or SIGINT), target exit, or SIGINT/SIGTERM disables tracing, drains remaining buffered lines within budget, reads per_cpu loss counters, detaches all session uprobes and the tracefs instance, and emits the report summary (windows, events, lost).

JSON schema (operation: "live_trace", schema_version: 1)

--json emits a single-line JSON document with stable static VAs (PIE slide removed) suitable for offline comparison (trace diff):

Field notes:

  • summary.stop_reason: "max_windows" | "max_events" | "duration_elapsed" | "interrupted" | "process_exited" | "process_changed".
  • summary.return_mode: "callsite" | "uretprobe_best_effort" | "mixed_uretprobe_best_effort".
  • windows[].status: "complete" (closed cleanly by --stop-return or --stop without missed inner frames), "incomplete" (missed inner return detected under stack unwind or loss), or "truncated" (cut off by --max-events, duration/signal/exit, or re-entered --start without --stop-return; incomplete_reason explains why).
  • windows[].events[].kind: "entry" | "return" | "stop". All target_va, call_site_va, and caller_va values are static image VAs formatted as lowercase 0x... hex strings with the runtime PIE slide removed.
